title: Rules vs Learning
description: Every robot behaviour you've built so far follows a rule you wrote by hand. This module is about robots that build their own rules from examples instead.

content.value: Two Completely Different Ways to Decide

Every program you've written this course follows a rule-based approach: you, the programmer, worked out exactly what to check and exactly what to do — if distance() < 30, turn. The robot never had to figure anything out; it just followed your instructions precisely, every time.

A learned approach flips that around. Instead of a human writing the exact rule, a program is shown thousands of examples and works out its own pattern for responding — one that a human never explicitly wrote down and might not even be able to fully explain.

content.title: 🆚 Same broken line, two approaches
content.hint: Press Run and watch what happens to each robot at the gap.

content.value: The rule-based robot's rule was exact: "if the line is under the sensor, go straight." The instant the line physically disappears at the gap, that rule has nothing to work with, and the robot stops. A model trained on many tracks — including ones with gaps — has effectively learned a softer, more general pattern: something closer to "keep going the way the line was heading, even for a moment without seeing it." Nobody wrote that rule by hand; it emerged from the training examples.

Neither approach is simply "better." A rule-based robot is fully predictable and easy to debug — you can read exactly why it did what it did. A learned one can handle situations nobody explicitly planned for, but it's much harder to know exactly why it made a particular choice.

Key takeaway: rule-based behaviour follows exact instructions a human wrote. Learned behaviour follows a pattern discovered from examples — able to handle situations no one explicitly planned for, at the cost of being harder to fully explain.

quiz.question: Why does the rule-based line follower stop at the gap in the track?
options: Its exact rule (line under sensor -> go straight) has nothing to work with once the line disappears
It runs out of battery exactly at gaps
Rule-based robots can't move in a straight line at all
quiz.explain: The rule was written for the case where the line is visible — a gap simply wasn't accounted for.

quiz.question: Where does a learned model's response to a gap actually come from?
options: A programmer wrote an explicit rule for gaps
A pattern discovered from many training examples, including tracks with gaps — not an explicit hand-written rule
quiz.explain: Nobody wrote "handle gaps this way" by hand — the behaviour emerged from what the model was trained on.

quiz.question: What's a genuine advantage of a rule-based approach over a learned one?
options: It's fully predictable and easy to explain exactly why it did something
It always performs better in every situation
It requires no programming at all
quiz.explain: Every rule-based decision traces back to a line of code you can read. That transparency is a real, genuine trade-off in the learned approach's favour.
